strengths: Significance: SALSA-V addresses useful practical needs in video-to-audio generation: temporal synchronization, reference-audio conditioning, iterative extension, and few-step sampling within one model.

Soundness: Table 1 provides promising evidence of improved synchronization. SALSA-V achieves DeSync of 0.497 versus MMAudio’s 0.521, and human synchronization MOS of 3.52 versus 2.92, with fewer reported generative-model parameters. Other objective metrics are broadly competitive.

The shortcut results are encouraging: Figure 5 shows little degradation at eight sampling steps, while Table 2 shows that shortcut training preserves approximately the same 32-step performance as ordinary flow matching at two model sizes.

Originality: The contribution primarily integrates established techniques, but applying shortcut training to video-to-audio generation and combining VideoPrism-based synchronization features with masked audio conditioning offers a potentially useful systems contribution.

Presentation and limitations: The architecture and qualitative examples are generally understandable. The paper explicitly acknowledges lower subjective audio quality than MMAudio and difficulties across scene cuts; this appropriately qualifies its practical applicability.
weaknesses: Soundness—attribution: The experiments do not isolate the proposed synchronization encoder, masking objective, or modified architecture. Changes to the visual backbone, training data, and fine-tuned audio VAE could explain the observed gains. Table 2 only varies model size and training objective; a controlled comparison against Synchformer conditioning and a masking ablation are needed to establish the contributions’ individual value.

Evaluation reliability: The mixed test set lacks sample counts, exact composition, reproducible splits, and sufficient information about baseline handling of variable durations and text conditioning. The listening study uses only ten selected videos and reports no confidence intervals or statistical analysis. Appendix A.3’s '180 individual scores' is ambiguous given 18 participants, ten trials, three systems, and three rating dimensions. Small objective improvements and the 0.14 overall-MOS gain therefore do not establish the claimed significant superiority.

Long-form evidence: Figure 5 compares iterative ten-second SALSA-V windows against MMAudio processing complete sequences beyond its training horizon. This demonstrates robustness relative to that particular baseline configuration, but does not isolate the benefit over comparable chunked generation. Relevant long-form methods discussed in the paper, such as V-AURA and LoVA, are not evaluated. Tests stop at 60 seconds, and FAD/DeSync do not directly measure boundary artifacts, persistent sound identity, or long-range coherence, leaving 'seamless' and unconstrained-length generation insufficiently supported.

Efficiency evidence: No wall-clock latency, real-time factor, memory usage, or end-to-end conditioning cost is reported, so fewer sampling steps do not establish near-real-time operation. The few-step comparison also omits SALSA-V’s own ordinary-flow-matching variant at reduced step counts and the efficiency-focused Frieren baseline, weakening attribution of the speed-quality advantage to shortcut training.

Reproducibility and methodological precision: Equation 2 names but does not explicitly construct the consistency target or specify the joint timestep/step-size sampling procedure. Data filtering thresholds, exact dataset manifests, several architectural dimensions, and VAE fine-tuning settings are missing. The masking range is also inconsistent: Section 3.2 gives 5 ms–2.5 s, whereas Appendix A.4 gives 1–88 tokens, approximately 23 ms–2.05 s at 43 Hz.

Audio-conditioning validation: Appendix A.2 uses an unspecified selected subset with recurring sound sources and no comparative conditioning baseline. Its spectral-distance description incorrectly treats normalized log-mel values as probability masses without ensuring nonnegativity, and describes sliced Wasserstein distance as an approximation converging to full Wasserstein distance. These issues weaken the interpretation and reproducibility of the supporting metric.

Research ethics and data transparency: The studio Foley dataset’s provenance, licensing, and availability are unspecified, and the listening study does not report consent or compensation procedures. These omissions warrant clarification; the manuscript does not otherwise provide evidence of a material ethical violation.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses useful practical problems in video-to-audio generation: temporal synchronization, few-step sampling, and reference-conditioned extension. Combining these capabilities could benefit Foley and sound-design workflows.

Soundness: The reported results are promising. Table 1 shows better synchronization than MMAudio, both objectively (DeSync 0.497 versus 0.521) and subjectively (3.52 versus 2.92), with fewer generator parameters. Figure 5 suggests substantially better robustness to reduced sampling budgets.

Originality: Integrating shortcut training into video-to-audio generation and developing VideoPrism-based synchronization features constitute plausible application-level contributions. Table 2 provides useful evidence that shortcut training preserves performance at 32 sampling steps.

Presentation and limitations: The architecture and conditioning mechanisms are generally understandable, and the qualitative examples illustrate their intended behavior. The authors appropriately acknowledge lower subjective audio quality than MMAudio and difficulty extending across scene cuts.
weaknesses: Soundness—insufficient isolation of the contributions: There is no controlled replacement of the proposed synchronization features with Synchformer features, nor an ablation of contrastive training or batch composition. Improvements could arise from the different pretrained backbones, additional training data, or modified VAE. Table 2 evaluates shortcut versus ordinary flow matching only at 32 steps; the crucial few-step comparison instead uses MMAudio, leaving the shortcut objective's incremental benefit within SALSA-V unestablished.

Evaluation reproducibility: Section 4 describes a custom mixture of test sources without reporting sample counts, exact splits, per-source results, or enough information to reconstruct the benchmark. The general test set contains videos up to 30 seconds, whereas Figure 5 includes 60-second videos from a separate, insufficiently specified set. Filtering thresholds, the studio Foley dataset, and training/evaluation overlap checks are also insufficiently documented. These omissions materially hinder verification of the headline results.

Long-form claims exceed the evidence: Figure 5 compares iterative SALSA-V extension with MMAudio processing the entire sequence beyond its training lengths. This demonstrates an advantage over that particular extrapolation strategy, but does not establish superiority over practical chunked baselines or relevant long-form methods such as V-AURA and LoVA. Evaluation reaches only 60 seconds and does not directly measure boundary artifacts, long-range consistency, or listener judgments of continuity. Consequently, 'seamless' generation of unconstrained length is not adequately supported.

Statistical support is inadequate: The listening study uses 18 participants and only 10 selected videos, with no confidence intervals or analysis accounting for repeated ratings of the same clips. Appendix A.3's '180 individual scores' is ambiguous because each trial rates three tracks on three dimensions. Table 1 provides no uncertainty, and the shaded bands in Figures 5–6 are not defined. The small objective improvements and overall-rating difference of 3.43 versus 3.29 therefore do not substantiate claims of significant superiority.

Efficiency claims lack measurements: Eight sampling steps do not establish near-real-time operation. The paper reports no wall-clock latency, real-time factor, inference hardware, peak memory, or end-to-end cost including visual feature extraction and audio decoding. The claimed practical efficiency advantage remains unverified.

Methodological reproducibility remains incomplete despite the appendix: Equation 2 does not explicitly define the consistency target or the sampling distribution over valid time/step-size pairs. Important implementation choices for masked shortcut training and inference are left implicit. Mask lengths also differ between Section 3.2's 5 ms–2.5 s and Appendix A.4's 1–88 tokens at 43 Hz. The sample-availability sentence contains no usable link, and no code or checkpoint access is specified.

Audio-conditioning evidence is narrow: Appendix A.2 evaluates an unspecified selected subset where the relevant sounds occur in both the reference and target portions. This supports continuation of recurring sounds, but provides limited evidence for broader reference-based sound control. The SWSD explanation also incorrectly treats normalized log-mel values as necessarily forming probability masses and describes sliced Wasserstein distance as an increasingly accurate approximation to full Wasserstein distance; additional projections estimate the sliced quantity instead.

Research ethics reporting is limited: The manuscript does not explain permissions or licensing for the collected video and studio Foley data, or consent and compensation arrangements for the listening study. These are reporting gaps rather than evidence of misconduct, but should be addressed.

strengths: Significance: SALSA-V addresses a useful combination of video-to-audio capabilities: temporal synchronization, reference-audio conditioning, iterative extension, and few-step sampling. Supporting these within one model could benefit interactive Foley workflows.

Soundness: The reported results provide encouraging evidence of synchronization improvements. Table 1 reports human synchronization scores of 3.52 versus MMAudio’s 2.92, alongside improved DeSync, FAD, and KLPaSST. Figure 5 also shows substantially better robustness to reduced sampling budgets and generation lengths up to 60 seconds.

Originality: Although the individual techniques build on existing work, combining shortcut training with masked video-conditioned flow matching is a useful application-level contribution. The VideoPrism-based synchronization encoder is another potentially valuable component.

Presentation and limitations: The architecture and intended conditioning mechanisms are generally understandable. The paper candidly acknowledges lower subjective audio quality than MMAudio and difficulties extending across scene cuts; these disclosures appropriately clarify the method’s scope.
weaknesses: Soundness—evaluation reliability: Section 4 does not specify the objective test-set size, source proportions, exact selection protocol, or construction of the dedicated long-form subset. The listening study uses only 10 selected videos and 18 participants, with no uncertainty estimates or analysis accounting for repeated ratings by listeners and videos. Figure 5 includes shaded bands without explaining their meaning. Consequently, claims of significant superiority are insufficiently supported, particularly for small differences such as DeSync 0.497 versus 0.521 and FAD 1.07 versus 1.12.

Soundness—missing component attribution: Table 2 varies model size and training objective only at 32 sampling steps. It does not compare shortcut and ordinary flow matching at low step counts, where the proposed objective should matter most. There is also no controlled replacement of the new synchronization encoder with Synchformer, or ablation of masking and codec changes. Improvements therefore cannot be attributed reliably to the proposed components rather than different representations, data, or codec training.

Significance—long-form claims exceed the comparisons: Figure 5 compares iterative 10-second generation against MMAudio processing increasingly long sequences directly, which the manuscript itself identifies as outside MMAudio’s training regime. This establishes a useful practical capability but does not establish superiority over appropriate long-form approaches. LoVA and V-AURA are discussed but not evaluated, and there is no chunked-baseline comparison or direct assessment of boundary artifacts and long-range consistency. Evidence through 60 seconds on single-shot videos does not substantiate seamless quality at unconstrained lengths.

Efficiency claims lack measurements: Eight sampling steps do not establish near-real-time operation. The paper reports no wall-clock latency, real-time factor, peak memory, or end-to-end cost including visual feature extraction and decoding. Parameter counts alone are insufficient to assess the practical efficiency of the full pipeline.

Reproducibility: Appendix A.4 provides useful optimizer and training details, but important specifications remain absent: the shortcut target construction and step-size sampling, filtering thresholds and dataset manifests, the studio Foley dataset’s availability, and detailed baseline inference handling. The audio-mask ranges also disagree: Section 3.2 gives 5 ms–2.5 s, whereas Appendix A.4 gives 1–88 tokens, approximately 23 ms–2.05 s at 43 Hz. The sample URL is blank, and no code or checkpoint access is supplied in the manuscript.

Presentation and interpretation: Appendix A.3 defines the human 'Overall Fit' question as semantic correspondence, while the main text interprets its score as overall quality. The separate audio-quality score actually favors MMAudio, 3.16 versus 2.96. This distinction matters to the claimed quality advantage. Appendix A.2 also describes normalized log-mel vectors as probability mass functions without ensuring nonnegative values; the sliced-Wasserstein calculation can operate on real vectors, but this probability interpretation is not justified.

Research ethics: No clear ethical violation is evident, but the manuscript does not explain licensing or permissions for the collected YouTube and studio audio, or consent and compensation for listening-study participants. These reporting gaps should be addressed. Overall, the promising integration and reported results do not yet outweigh the material evaluation and reproducibility weaknesses.

strengths: Significance: SALSA-V addresses a useful combination of practical requirements: synchronized Foley generation, reference-audio conditioning, iterative extension, and efficient sampling. Combining these capabilities in one model could benefit interactive sound-design workflows.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports competitive results with a 643M-parameter generator: FAD of 1.07 versus MMAudio’s 1.12, ImageBind alignment of 33.76 versus 32.89, and DeSync of 0.497 versus 0.521. The human synchronization score improves more substantially, from 2.92 to 3.52.

Efficiency: Figure 4 provides encouraging evidence that quality remains relatively stable at eight sampling steps. Table 3 shows improvements over four-step Frieren across the reported metrics, while Table 2 suggests that shortcut training does not materially degrade performance at 32 steps.

Originality: The contribution is primarily a useful integration of established techniques. Applying shortcut training to video-to-audio generation and combining VideoPrism-based synchronization features with masked flow matching constitute a plausible application-level advance.

Presentation and responsible reporting: The manuscript is generally readable, with informative architectural diagrams and qualitative examples. It explicitly acknowledges sound carryover across scene cuts and discusses deceptive-media risks. These disclosures are appropriate and are not themselves weaknesses.
weaknesses: Soundness—insufficiently specified evaluation: Section 4 does not report the test-set size, dataset proportions, exact selection protocol, or how duration-limited baselines process the mixed-length inputs. The test set is described as containing videos up to 30 seconds, whereas Figure 4 evaluates 60-second examples without explaining their provenance. These omissions make the main comparisons difficult to reproduce and their fairness difficult to assess.

Soundness—missing controlled ablations: The claimed synchronization contribution is not tested by replacing the proposed features with Synchformer features under otherwise identical conditions. Neither the smaller contrastive batch-size argument nor the modified VAE is isolated experimentally. Likewise, the matched flow-matching and shortcut models are compared only at 32 steps, rather than across the few-step regime central to the shortcut claim. Comparisons against differently trained architectures do not establish which proposed components cause the improvements.

Long-form claims exceed the evidence: Figure 4 compares chunked SALSA-V against MMAudio processing the entire sequence, explicitly beyond its training lengths. A chunked baseline with overlap or crossfading is needed to establish the benefit of learned outpainting over straightforward extension. The LoVA comparison is useful, but FAD and DeSync do not directly assess audible boundary artifacts, persistent sound identity, or long-range coherence. No dedicated long-form listening study supports the claims of seamless, unconstrained-length generation.

Mathematical specification requires correction: In Equation 3, the second teacher evaluation uses time t for the advanced state x′ at t+d; the stated two-step consistency construction requires evaluating at t+d. The listed step sizes, 32, 16, ..., 1, are also inconsistent with their use as integration increments in Equation 4 unless an unreported conversion is applied. The time distribution and joint sampling of valid time/step-size pairs are insufficiently specified. These may be notation errors, but they affect reproduction of the central training objective.

Statistical support and claim calibration: The human study uses only 10 selected videos and 18 listeners, without confidence intervals or an analysis accounting for repeated ratings by video and listener. Overall scores differ modestly, 3.43 versus 3.29, and SALSA-V’s audio-quality score is lower than MMAudio’s, 2.96 versus 3.16. The objective DeSync improvement is also small. Claims of significant superiority therefore need stronger statistical support; Figure 4’s shaded bands are not explained.

Audio-conditioning evidence is limited: Appendix A.3 evaluates a selected subset containing recurring sounds but gives neither its size nor selection details sufficient for replication. Algorithm 1 normalizes log-mel values by their sum, which does not generally produce the claimed nonnegative probability vectors. Sliced Wasserstein distance can operate on real-valued vectors, but the stated probability interpretation and normalization need correction. This experiment does not establish broad reference-sound transfer or preservation of perceptual identity.

Reproducibility: The appendix supplies useful optimization details, but the studio Foley dataset, filtering thresholds, data-mixture proportions, and evaluation prompts remain unspecified; the project-page field is blank. The masking range also differs between Section 3.2 and Appendix A.5. Table 4 does not clarify whether timing includes visual feature extraction and audio decoding, limiting the end-to-end near-real-time claim. Together with the evaluation and objective ambiguities, these gaps prevent reliable independent verification.

strengths: Significance: SALSA-V addresses useful practical needs in video-to-audio synthesis: temporal synchronization, reference-audio conditioning, iterative extension, and fast sampling. Combining these capabilities in one model could benefit Foley workflows.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports competitive results with a 643M-parameter generator, including FAD 1.07 versus MMAudio’s 1.12 and synchronization MOS 3.52 versus 2.92. Figure 4 suggests substantially better robustness to reduced sampling budgets, and Table 3 reports improvements over reflow-trained Frieren across all six metrics at four steps.

Originality: The contribution is primarily a useful integration of established techniques, with potentially valuable domain-specific advances through VideoPrism-based synchronization features and shortcut training for audio generation. Table 2 supports the narrower claim that shortcut training preserves performance at 32 steps.

Presentation and responsible reporting: The paper is generally readable, with helpful architectural diagrams and qualitative examples. It explicitly acknowledges difficulties across scene cuts and discusses deceptive-media risks. Appendix A.3 appropriately excludes conditioning audio from the evaluated generated region.
weaknesses: Soundness—central contributions are insufficiently isolated. There is no controlled replacement of the proposed synchronization encoder with Synchformer, no masking/outpainting ablation, and no few-step comparison against the otherwise identical flow-matching model. Table 2 only evaluates the latter at 32 steps. Consequently, the results do not establish how much improvement comes from the proposed components versus different training data, pretrained backbones, or the modified VAE.

Evaluation reproducibility and comparability are materially incomplete. Section 4 does not specify the composite test set’s size, source proportions, exact splits, or baseline handling of variable-length inputs. Dataset filtering uses unspecified relative thresholds, and the studio Foley dataset is insufficiently documented. The stated test videos extend to 30 seconds, yet Figure 4 evaluates 60-second examples without explaining their provenance. These omissions make the principal comparisons difficult to reproduce and assess.

Long-form claims exceed the evidence. Figure 4 compares SALSA-V’s iterative 10-second generation against MMAudio run on entire sequences beyond its training lengths; the manuscript itself identifies unseen positional embeddings as a reason for MMAudio’s deterioration. A practical chunked baseline is needed to assess the benefit of learned continuation. The LoVA comparison at 30 seconds is useful, but neither it nor aggregate FAD/DeSync establishes seamless boundaries, persistent sound identity, or quality over unrestricted durations. The disclosed scene-cut limitation is appropriate; the concern is the breadth of the remaining claims.

Statistical support for superiority is weak. The listening study uses only 10 selected videos and 18 participants, without confidence intervals or an analysis accounting for listener and clip variation. Appendix A.4’s statement of '180 individual scores' is ambiguous given three tracks and three rating dimensions per trial. Table 1’s overall-fit improvement is modest, while audio-quality MOS is lower than MMAudio’s (2.96 versus 3.16). The small mean DeSync improvement (0.521 to 0.497 seconds) also needs uncertainty analysis. Figure 4 includes shaded bands without defining them.

The shortcut formulation has consequential ambiguities. Equation 3 evaluates the second half-step at time t rather than t+d, which does not express the stated two-step consistency target for a time-dependent field. Section 3.3 lists step sizes as 32, 16, ..., 1, although Equation 4 requires integration increments, and specifies log-normal time sampling without explaining its mapping to the flow interval. These may be notation errors, but the implemented objective and sampling procedure must be clarified before the method is reliably reproducible.

The audio-conditioning evidence is preliminary. Appendix A.3 uses an unspecified selected subset without a competing conditioning method. Its SWSD explanation also contains mathematical errors: normalizing log-mel values by their sum does not generally produce probability mass functions, and increasing the number of projections estimates sliced Wasserstein distance rather than recovering the full Wasserstein distance. These issues weaken the interpretation of the claimed spectral-preservation evidence.

Overall assessment: The manuscript presents a promising and potentially useful system, but missing controls, an underspecified evaluation protocol, and implementation ambiguities prevent confident acceptance. Additional documentation should also clarify studio-data provenance and permissions, participant consent and recruitment, and whether reported latency includes conditioning-feature extraction and decoding. The decisive concerns are evidential soundness and reproducibility, rather than the acknowledged limitations or incremental character of the method.

strengths: Significance: SALSA-V addresses useful practical requirements together: synchronized video-to-audio generation, reference-audio conditioning, iterative extension, and few-step sampling. This combination could benefit Foley and sound-design workflows.

Soundness: The reported results are promising across several complementary metrics. Table 1 improves DeSync over MMAudio from 0.521 to 0.497 and human synchronization ratings from 2.92 to 3.52. Table 5 also reports consistent improvements over LoVA on 30-second clips.

Efficiency: Figure 4 indicates that quality and synchronization remain stable at eight sampling steps. Table 3 provides a comparison against a dedicated few-step Frieren checkpoint, while Table 4 reports 0.71 seconds to generate ten seconds of audio at four steps on an A100.

Originality: Although the components build on established approaches, combining shortcut training, masked audio conditioning, and VideoPrism-based synchronization features is a useful systems contribution. Table 2 supports compatibility between shortcut training and full-step generation quality.

Presentation and limitations: The architecture and qualitative examples are generally clear, and the appendix provides substantial training details. The discussion candidly identifies difficulties with scene changes, and the impact statement acknowledges deceptive-media risks.
weaknesses: Evaluation reproducibility is insufficient for the central comparisons. The custom mixed-duration test set lacks sample counts, source proportions, identifiers, and a clear protocol for handling each baseline's duration limits and text conditioning. Section 4 describes test videos of up to 30 seconds, whereas Figure 4 evaluates 60-second examples without explaining their provenance. These omissions prevent reliable interpretation and replication of the headline results.

The ablations do not isolate the main claimed mechanisms. There is no controlled replacement of the proposed synchronization encoder with Synchformer, no batch-composition ablation supporting the hard-negative argument, and no separation of the effects of training data and the modified VAE. Table 2 compares objectives only at 32 steps; evaluating the same vanilla flow-matching model at fewer steps is necessary to attribute the few-step gains specifically to shortcut training.

The long-form evidence does not establish seamless extension or sustained contextual consistency. MMAudio is evaluated on full sequences beyond its training lengths, while SALSA-V uses short windows. A windowed baseline and an ablation without reference-audio overlap would better establish the value of the proposed extension mechanism. FAD and DeSync do not directly measure boundary artifacts or sound-identity drift, and no long-form listening evaluation is reported.

The strength of the synchronization and overall-quality claims exceeds the statistical evidence. The listening study covers only ten selected videos and 18 participants, with no confidence intervals or paired analysis. Appendix A.4 reports 180 individual scores despite three systems and three rating dimensions per trial, leaving the counting unclear. Moreover, SALSA-V's audio-quality MOS is lower than MMAudio's, 2.96 versus 3.16, so the human results support a synchronization benefit rather than uniformly improved quality.

Methodological notation needs correction for reproducibility. Equation 3 evaluates the second shortcut prediction at time t despite advancing the state to t+d. Step size d is illustrated with integers 32, 16, ..., 1 rather than clarified as an integration interval, and the stated log-normal time sampling lacks a mapping to the flow interval. The masking range also differs between Section 3.2 and Appendix A.5. These may be reporting errors, but the intended implementation is ambiguous.

The audio-conditioning evaluation is preliminary: Appendix A.3 uses an unspecified selected subset, and Algorithm 1 calls normalization of potentially negative log-mel values probability normalization. Its random-projection average estimates sliced Wasserstein distance, not the full Wasserstein distance as the prose suggests. Data-filtering thresholds, the studio Foley dataset's provenance and availability, and whether runtime includes visual feature extraction also need clarification. Overall, the contribution has clear merits, but stronger controls and a reproducible evaluation protocol are needed before acceptance.
